claimed: /menu returns HTTP 404 — the menu page is broken
actual: The menu works fine in a browser. The site builder uses client-side routing, so a direct path request 404s at the server while the in-app nav renders normally.
reason: The crawler is not a browser. It does not run JS and cannot follow client-side routes, so it reported a real HTTP status that is not what a customer experiences.
proposedRule: A bare HTTP status code from a site builder usually means client-side routing the crawler could not follow. A rendered 404 page with its own copy means the route is genuinely missing. Only the second is safe to lead with.

claimed: Site returns 'Too many redirects' — confirmed on five attempts across two days
actual: Site loads normally in a browser. The real gap is that there is no menu on the site at all; the only route in is the Order Online button.
reason: Repeated identical machine readings felt like confirmation but were the same blind spot repeated. Re-fetching does not validate a fetch-based claim.
proposedRule: When a gap claim fails verification, look for the real gap before discarding the lead — the opener is wrong, not necessarily the lead. Also: a design opinion ('menu and photos on separate screens') is not a defect and makes a weak opener.

claimed: Wix placeholder content, San Francisco demo address, no menu — a neglected site
actual: The page reading was accurate and is unchanged. But this is a site MID-BUILD, not a neglected one — the Mammoth Poke team is likely building it right now.
reason: An unfinished site and a neglected site look identical from outside and mean opposite things commercially. The observation was right; the inference was wrong.
proposedRule: Before leading with a placeholder or template-default gap, check whether the business recently opened, changed hands, or has a builder attached. If it opened in the last ~60 days, assume mid-build unless proven otherwise.

claimed: v1 drafts listed every defect found and did not say how the sender came to be looking at the page
actual: Rewritten to five beats: route disclosed, one customer-visible wall, mechanical consequence, who you are, permission-style ask.
reason: Disclosing no route and listing multiple defects reads as surveillance — like a compiled report rather than something a person happened to hit. Also: lead with the most CUSTOMER-VISIBLE defect, not the most damning one.
proposedRule: Five-beat structure, one defect only, blame the gap and never the owner, rotate beat 4 phrasing across a batch so owners comparing notes don't see identical paragraphs.

claimed: IG status marked 'active (est.)' based on a search-indexed post
actual: For two leads the only indexed post was 1-5 years old despite the businesses clearly being active.
reason: Search-indexed Instagram posts skew old even for accounts that post weekly, so an old indexed post is evidence of nothing either way.
proposedRule: When the only evidence of IG activity is an indexed post more than a year old, status is 'unconfirmed', not 'active-est'.
